questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Even though I had this university/destination as my 4th priority, it should've been way higher if I had known what I was getting into.
TSE (Toulouse School of Economics), a part-independent institution under Université Toulouse Capitole, ranks among the top 10 of the world's best universities in economics. The level is similar to that of the University of Copenhagen, but they have many exciting courses - one in Environmental economics, which I took. 
Toulouse, the fourth biggest city in France, is beautiful and situated in the very centre of the south of France. It looks like it's a huge city on Google Maps, but it's very easy to get around the city by bike (Swap-fiets or rental), metro or bus. The city is full of students from all over the world and has many nice restaurants (low prices), bars and nightclubs.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't easy sometimes.
The University of Toulouse is huge and has several buildings situated apart from each other, resulting in some problems when first arriving since you have no idea what the place is called and where each room or auditory is. 
I got a map from the information desk at Arsénal, which helped a lot! Furthermore, whenever in doubt, I wrote e-mails to the exchange coordinator at the University of Toulouse. I would send too many e-mails than too few. 
There can go a couple of days before you get your student-card and the deadline of when to apply for courses which can be stressful - but again: Write to the exchange coordinator if you're in doubt about anything!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
You get an invitation e-mail from the university to attend a welcoming meeting with all the other ERASMUS students.
At that meeting, you'll be provided with 90% of the information needed throughout your stay regarding the school and social events hosted by ERASMUS.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Before the stay, I agreed with four others to try to find a place where we could live.
We arrived one week before school started. 
We lived in three different places before we could find more permanent housing. First, we lived at a hostel outside the city for 4 days, then moved to an AirBnB in the city centre for four days and then another AirBnB in another location for four-five days until we found the best permanent location ever!
I recommend looking for accommodation at least three months before! You should apply in Facebook groups e.g: "TOULOUSE: location apartment et colocation" and also search on Google.
Some of the web-sites are: Lebocoin, Les Carter des coloc, apartager and chez nestor.
REMEMBER! The renter has always the right to terminate the lease of the accommodation - so I recommend lying about how long you will stay depending on what the landlord are interested in (Everyone does it). 

We lived in a house at 28 Rue Pierre Cazeneuve with five bedrooms, three toilets, a big kitchen, a laundry room, a garden and two offices. We paid 580 euros pr. person, which was perfect for us. Contact 'Agestis Agency' and ask if it is available. You can ask for Arnaud, who was our contact person within the agency, and say that you were recommended the house by the five danish guys.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I liked it very much! You get a better view of the city than being situated around the universities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You go to the invitational meeting, where you get the info. If in doubt about the information given, then write an e-mail to the exchange coordinator.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: In person regarding the university. ANY questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
When you apply for the location first, you type in the courses you want to take; however, it is not certain that you will get the course once the registration opens. Registration opens once you're in Toulouse. 
You must get their course list for exchange students for courses in M1 and M2 (master 1&2) since these can differ greatly in level and type.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The first two weeks at the university, you can try out a lot of different courses - thus, attend a bunch of lectures in different courses that are open for Erasmus students and choose once the registration opens.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses can vary a lot. But the mean level is approximately the same as that of UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Very similar. However, depending on the course, you use your computer way less, whereas everything is written in hand. Also, note that I had to write all exams by hand. 
Some lecturers use chalk and board teaching some use PP slides.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Valuing the Environment 
Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy
Sustainable Development
Macroeconomics
Causal Inference
Market Power and Regulation

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All of the courses I wrote above are very nice. 
Since these courses are quite rare, I would especially recommend the environmental courses: Valuing the Environment, Sustainable development and Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy. And the professors are very skilled.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I broke my foot at Futsal, so I had my foot in a cast for 1,5 months - so a lot of hospital bills however, these are covered by insurance.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Grocery stores are way more expensive than I thought. 
Restaurants and red wine are very cheap.
A cheap bar is Café Populaire, where some nights they have a happy day offer where you can get 13 drinks for 13 euros. That was quite nice :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The university has ALL the sports you can imagine from indoor climbing to fencing to football to Krav Maga. 
Though you have to remember to buy the sport-gear yourself. 
For social activities, ERASMUS host 1-2 parties a week, BDE (Toulouse School of Economics parties) host monthly parties and ERASMUS hosts a trip outside of Toulouse every other week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I played on the universities football and futsal team - until I broke by foot. People are not very good at outdoor football, but the futsal was quite a high level.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go on the ERASMUS trips, go partying with the other students, take a walk around Toulouse, try the metro, go out to eat at a restaurant, go bowling (very fun). 
Eat a lot of cheese, duck and wine. You're not on exchange to lose weight.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The French are quite arrogant and don't speak very great English. So expect to spend your time with the other ERASMUS students. If you want to learn french, there are plenty of french-language schools, and you can speak to french people. You can meet french people through sports activities, Tinder and in the nightlife.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Be kind. 
Smile a lot and try to speak french. 
You can try to move in at a co-location with local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not differences you haven't seen before - we're all human.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The French cuisine.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Have fun
Go out
Meet a lot of new people

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is very hot in the summer and can be zero degrees in the winter - so bring a diverse wardrobe.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: You get a lot better at english and the school is very good.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The information before and during the exchange was awful. 
You are acting as a middle-man between the two universities, which I thought was very stressful. One didn't even go on exchange because of the information overload. Some e-mails don't matter, while some are very important with strict deadlines. Be calm and call the universities if you're in doubt about anything.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
